The characters of the family don’t know how to counter Derek’s “logic-backed” racist screeds, and neither do the writers of the movie. They just don’t understand debating fascism away is impossible: this assumes it operates on the basis of logic, instead of rationalisations, rewriting history and suppression of dissent. Even then, the arguments they put forward are so weak, apparently all it takes for a nazi to have a change of heart is a sassy black friend and getting sexually assaulted. It’s no wonder that neonazis see Derek as inspirational and use the movie to recruit; they aren’t missing the point, it’s just unconvincing. And that ending is such a slap in the face too, equating black hoodlums to neonazis and placing tantamount responsibility on both sides. “hate is baggage” my ass Racism isn’t just hate, it’s contempt and disgust, which poses a certain group of people beneath another in a made-up hierarchy, and has justified the worst crimes in history. Hating fascists doesn’t perpetuate cycles of hatred, rather it’s a necessary premise to fight them.

There is a particular scene in American History X where the family gathers around the dinner table and begins discussing Rodney King, and it was around that moment that I realized what sort of movie I was watching. One of those deeply reflective American dramas attempting to examine society, prejudice, violence and the consequences of hatred through the experiences of its characters. While I recognize the importance of the subject, I found the confrontation itself surprisingly clumsy in its execution. The editing is choppy, the camerawork feels awkward and the entire argument unfolds with a rather disjointed rhythm that undermines what should have been an intense family confrontation. Given how important this scene is in exposing the prejudices already present within Derek’s household, I would have appreciated considerably more control over its presentation. And although I acknowledge some of the arguments the movie raises, I cannot say the experience particularly moved or inspired me. What I found rather strange was the family’s apparent struggle to understand how Derek became such an extreme racist. His father had already demonstrated deeply prejudiced attitudes, influencing the way Derek understood the world long before his eventual radicalization. The mother married a man who held those beliefs, yet the family seems almost bewildered by how far that influence eventually extends. Perhaps there is something worth examining in how prejudice becomes normalized within a household until someone takes it to a horrifying extreme, but I found the treatment of that contradiction somewhat strange. Nevertheless, I think the movie does a respectable job of portraying indoctrination. The way resentment, selective information, political rhetoric and the influence of other people gradually shape someone’s beliefs is convincingly presented. Derek’s transformation into a violent extremist does not happen independently of his surroundings. His worldview is cultivated, reinforced and eventually exploited by people who encourage him to interpret entire communities through hostility and suspicion. However, I do not think the movie explores the hypocrisy within these hateful movements nearly as effectively as it could have. There are opportunities to expose the contradictions between their supposed principles, their conduct and the reality of the people they condemn, but I found the examination relatively limited. The movie is considerably more interested in portraying the destructive consequences of hatred than examining those contradictions in depth. I also find something rather ironic about the movie’s portrayal of Black characters. For a story that spends so much time confronting racist rhetoric and eventually attempts to challenge those prejudices, it is strange how many of the Black characters are portrayed through criminality, violence or incarceration. Why not show more ordinary Black Americans simply going about their lives, working, spending time with family, enjoying friendships and experiencing the same everyday pleasures and frustrations as anyone else? There could have been something genuinely heartwarming about Derek gradually witnessing the ordinary humanity of the very community he had been taught to despise. Instead, the movie remains so preoccupied with violence and criminality that it rarely explores those possibilities. This is precisely why I appreciate his friendship with Lamont so much. Derek’s developing relationship with the Black inmate he works alongside in the prison laundry is where I felt the movie became genuinely meaningful. Admittedly, even this friendship develops within a prison, but I don’t want that observation to diminish what I consider the strongest part of the entire experience. Their ordinary conversations, humour and growing familiarity communicate more about overcoming prejudice than another confrontation ever could. There is something wonderfully human about watching their relationship develop without requiring an elaborate philosophical argument or some extraordinary emotional revelation. Lamont doesn’t need to deliver a speech explaining why Derek’s beliefs are wrong. His personality, kindness and simple humanity gradually undermine the imaginary enemy Derek has constructed in his mind. The hostility begins to disappear as Derek discovers that the person standing beside him is not remotely the threatening figure his ideology has taught him to imagine. I would have loved to see that humanity extended beyond the prison walls, allowing Derek’s transformation to develop through everyday encounters rather than predominantly through suffering and violence. Watching him gradually recognize the ordinary lives, relationships and personalities of people he had spent so long despising could have provided a much more substantial examination of the prejudices he was beginning to abandon. For me, those interactions with Lamont already demonstrate how powerful that approach could have been. Personal experience begins replacing inherited prejudice, and the movie becomes considerably more affecting when it allows genuine human connection to challenge beliefs that had previously seemed impossible to question. The performances are respectable, particularly Edward Norton’s portrayal of Derek, although I never developed much emotional attachment to the characters themselves. The technical filmmaking is similarly adequate without being especially memorable. I found the editing somewhat uneven, the score underwhelming and the pacing occasionally frustrating, although the movie remains reasonably entertaining despite my reservations about its storytelling. The ending, however, left me questioning what the movie ultimately wanted to achieve through Danny’s murder. Was that final tragedy necessary for Derek to fully confront the consequences of the hatred and violence he had once embraced? Was the loss of his younger brother supposed to provide some final, devastating moment of realization after everything he had already experienced in prison? I struggled to understand what that conclusion added to his transformation, particularly when the friendship with Lamont had already demonstrated how convincingly personal experience could challenge his prejudices. The sudden violence felt like another bleak attempt to reinforce the destructive nature of hatred, and the school shooting itself struck me as an almost painfully familiar element of American tragedy. I would have found it considerably more interesting to explore what Derek actually does with his newfound understanding rather than confront him with yet another devastating consequence of the world he helped perpetuate. Ultimately, I think American History X raises worthwhile questions but does not explore them in a way I found particularly profound. I respect its intentions and recognize the importance of confronting racism and extremism, but I was far more interested in the possibility of overcoming indoctrination through genuine human connection than in another demonstration of the destruction hatred can cause. Its tragic conclusion did little to strengthen my appreciation, especially when the movie had already demonstrated a far more compelling direction through Derek’s friendship with Lamont. Their ordinary conversations and growing affection are what I will remember most fondly, because they show how personal familiarity can begin dismantling years of inherited prejudice without requiring another devastating act of violence. Nobody is born hating an entire race, community or group of people. Regardless of the headlines, statistics or political convictions used to justify those feelings, hatred and bigotry are learned, absorbed through our surroundings and passed from one generation to another. American History X ne condamne pas la xénophobie, il vend la lutte contre le racisme. Pour les points positifs, je note la remarquable performance d'Edward Norton. La photographie est bonne, les scènes en noirs et blanc sont très léchées visuellement. Et quelques scènes sont marquantes dans leur visuel. Maintenant, je pense que American History X s'est lancé sur un sujet trop abrupt, et ce qu'on en retient à la fin est manichéen : Leader n*** au début, militant anti-raciste à la fin. Comment? Par ce que il a rencontré un noir sympa en prison... Les noirs dans ce film sont soit des méchants gangsters soit des objets narratifs pour dé-raciser le protagoniste. J'avais trouvé intéressant l'aspect du chef des skinhead qui endoctrine les autres pour sa cause, mais ce n'est pas déconstruit par la suite ce qui laisse perplexe quant au fait que le personnage d'Edward Norton se détache aussi facilement de ces idées horribles. De plus, bien que leur idéologie est atroce, leurs actions ne le sont pas tant, ils sont presque représentés comme un groupe de potes, et à part quelques scènes de violence modérée on n'est pas horrifié, ce que j'avais trouvé dans Combat Girl, où on assistait à des scènes extrêmement choquantes qui nous font bien comprendre que c'est les grands méchants, ici non... Je pense que le principal problème de ce film est qu'il donne une vision unilatérale de la chose, que ça soit narrativement, car on ne suit qu'exclusivement le côté des néo-n***, ainsi que dans la mise en scène, comme si on voulait nous mettre dans leur monde, nous faire comprendre comment ils sont et comment ils vivent. Ce procédé peut être compréhensible dans certains films : par exemple un film de guerre où on pourrait nous plonger dans ce qu'on considérerait comme le camp des méchants, pour comprendre leurs intentions, leurs motivations, etc. Mais là c'est des néo-n*** ! La pire atrocité humaine que l'histoire n'ait connu ! Ce n'est donc pas normale de les dépeindre d'une manière aussi banale, même glamourisé (Avec un Edward Norton divinement beau et charismatique), alors que la réalité est bien plus atroce. Le résultat donne quelque chose qui ne semble pas immorale, auquel beaucoup de personnes dans ces temps où le racisme est en vogue, seront poussés à s'identifier (Preuve à l'appui : On trouve une flopée d'edit qui glorifie le personnage principal, et il suffit d'ouvrir les commentaires pour voir énormément de personnes qui disent même le préférer au début). Et le père de Derek, qui s'est fait tuer gratuitement (Le gentil pompier tué par un immigré sans motif), qui n'est jamais expliqué ou désamorcé, je note aussi la scène finale ou un afro américain abat froidement Danny qui est la cerise sur gâteau pour les facho, de quoi les laisser sur un goût amer qui détruira quoi qu'il advienne le peu d'antiracisme que le film contenait... Que c'est maladroit ! Peut être que ça passait il y'a 30 ans, mais plus aujourd'hui...

American History X (1998) — ★★★☆☆ edward norton gives a performance so good that it almost makes you forget you’re watching a film that occasionally seems determined to make its point by hitting you over the head with it. the black-and-white cinematography is effective, the shift between past and present works well, and norton is genuinely frightening as derek. he captures how someone can become consumed by hatred and convince himself that his cruelty is somehow justified. edward furlong is also excellent as danny, a younger brother desperately trying to understand the world through the ideology he’s been taught. the film’s strongest idea is that hatred doesn’t exist in isolation. it gets passed down, encouraged and normalised until people mistake it for identity. watching danny follow the same path as derek makes the story especially unsettling, because you can see how easily the cycle continues. but while i respect what the film is trying to say, i found some of its messaging a little heavy-handed. its characters can occasionally feel like they’re there to deliver the film’s arguments rather than exist beyond them, and the bluntness sometimes takes away from the complexity of the subject. still, the performances are powerful, and the film’s central warning remains important: hatred doesn’t make you strong, and realising you’ve been wrong doesn’t automatically undo the damage you’ve caused. three stars. a powerful film with an important message, even if it sometimes feels like it’s underlining that message three times.

Edward Norton is frightening in this. He doesn't actually have to hit anybody to get there. Derek can take over a dinner table and make racist garbage sound like some great truth everyone else is too scared to hear. I believe people would follow him. Norton doesn't soften that guy to make the one who comes home from prison easier to accept, either. He gets quieter and spends more time listening. I buy his fear for his brother completely. The prison flashbacks just don't show me how he became this thoughtful philosopher. I'm less certain what to make of the curb killing. It is unbearable, rightly so, and I don't want the movie to make Derek's violence easier to watch. But that scene has become the thing people remember the film for. It had overshadowed the rest of the movie in my memory, too. And you know what? Turns out the rest of the film is sort of a middling kludge of racial savior tropes. I get uncomfortable calling a movie like that an unmitigated success. Danny's school essay keeps explaining things I've just watched Norton get across with his face and his perfect abs. By the closing voiceover — ugg — I'm tired of being told what to take away from a performance that has already done the work. Let me sit with the guy for a minute and please, for the love of everything, can we agree that naming the movie the class title in the movie is dumb? I get much the same impatience with the slow motion and Anne Dudley's boys' choir. I'll be caught up in an ugly family argument, then feel the film working much too hard to impress on me how important all of this is. Kaye and Norton fought over the edit, and Norton helped shape the released version. I can't tell you which of them is responsible for what bothers me, but I'm absolutely not going to assume there's a great film hiding in Kaye's shorter cut any more than what's on screen in the released cut. Avery Brooks can give me the speech , though. I love him in this. Dr. Sweeney is written as the wise Black educator who arrives to help a white man understand his life, and Brooks makes me care about him even with that excruciatingly familiar job description. When he talks about his own anger, I want to hear him out . "Has anything you've done made your life better?" is an awfully direct way to state the movie's point but I am here for it . He's my Mr. Holland. What can I say? I need more between that conversation and the changed man Norton plays so well. His prison experience gives him reasons to question what he believes. I want to spend longer watching him try, especially after seeing how good he is at defending those beliefs. Lamont and Sweeney have a lot to undo. The breakfast conversation with his father feels WAY too convenient in the other direction. I can believe he picked up plenty from his dad, but I want more than that conversation to explain how he got so, so far. Watching in 2026, I'm also thinking about how much of that reinforcement can arrive through a screen, without anyone needing to join a gang. The father's influence and Cameron's recruiting haven't become irrelevant. They just feel like a limited account of a problem the movie is very confident it has explained. Norton and Brooks are worth seeing this for, even with all my complaints. I wish the movie would shut the hell up and let them work. Ce film est très bien réalisé et Edward Norton donne une performance vraiment folle, c’est un grand acteur. Le sujet abordé est délicat et je pense que certaines notes attribuées sont dûs aux thématiques du film, malheureusement encore d’actualité aujourd’hui. Effectivement c’est très « léger » que Derek ai convaincu aussi facilement son petit frère Dan à changer drastiquement d’opinion, et pas vraiment réaliste. En regardant le film, j’ai pensé que c’était un peu facile de faire en sorte que le personnage de Derek, raciste et nazi, change de mentalité et « devient une bonne personne » après s’être fait un ami noir en prison, comme si au final c’était la solution miracle qui mettrait fin au problématiques racistes dans le monde. Mais le moment où Derek comprend que son équipe de nazi en prison collabore en réalité avec des mexicains, ce qui « décrédibilise » toute leur idéologie, a montré la futilité de ce genre d’idéologie de haine. Tout est trop manichéen, j’aurais voulu que le film creuse d’avantage sur la construction/l’effondrement des croyances. J’ai aussi été un peu déçu par la facilité de la scène du déjeuner avec le père, lorsque Derek, un garçon tout à fait studieux et admiratif de son professeur, « découvre » le point de vu de son père par lequel il se fait influencer. Tough film to talk about. One quick look on this site and you can see a lot of people not just disliking it but being straight up against it. Some of the people I've seen holding this stance are also black people. It's hard to not be influenced when people, who the main character of the film and his ideology inflict so much pain to , are sharing their perspective on why American History X doesn't work. And I hear them wholeheartedly and respectfully. But I have a completely different perspective. I'm a white dude from Greece whose only contact with the racial tensions of the US has been through art and social media. Maybe if I ever truly see and live in that world firsthand maybe then my mind about the film will truly change. Right now I hear what people have to say but I have my own opinion. This movie is powerful. It did a number on me when I first saw it 10 years ago and it still does. Derek Vineyard is a fascinating character because of how real he feels. He is a smart dude who can hold his own in political debates and he also truly cares about his loved ones. But he is also a neonazi scumbag. We can truly see how through unchecked emotional and fatherly baggage he goes down that dark road even though he seems smart enough to know all of this is bullshit. Sure, in real life most racist pieces of shit are more like his fat friend who is an absolute dumbshit who just fucking sucks and does everything he does because he is just a fucking idiot. But the Vineyards are also out there and they are much scarier than any regular dumbass  skinhead. And Norton plays it scary. In all the flashback scenes he is intimidating and at times horrifying. Perfectly juxtaposed by his performance in the present in which he has a calm and caring aura without completely missing his inability to control his emotions. Although I can praise Norton all day for his performance I think there is a lot to be said about how the film accidentally glorifies his character and the violence he commits. Starting with his look. The choice to make him a jacked suave guy kinda muddles the waters because at times he legit can come through as a badass. And you don't want that. I think having him be more of an unfit and kinda slimy guy before his change of heart would avoid any misconception. And also maybe his fitness change happening after  prison would make it even more clear his character changed through his appearance. The hair growing is a nice touch but I think more could have been done. That said I think a lot of scenes needed less done to be better. What do I mean? Get rid of that slow motion. Tone down the music. A lot of the more brutal and shocking moments of the film kinda lose their punch because they feature all of the above when they truly don't need them. Let the scenes be as realistically portrayed as possible. Some of the most hard-hitting scenes are some where the characters are just talking that are played out as raw as possible. Just close ups to the actors faces and the reactions of everyone around them. That's the ticket. If the whole movie played out like this then we would have a completely non cheesy excellent film. As I said at the beginning American History X is a tough film. So much of it is rough around the edges but the core shines so much. It's truly timeless. The dad's monologue freaked me out. I hear that logic everyday on the internet. Almost verbatim. This "I'm not saying I'm racist but every other thing I say points to me being one" kinda weasely talk. Maybe I'm not the real authority on this movies success but what I get from it is special. The generational baggage, the undealt rage, the feeling that the whole world is out to get you, turning your life around. The movie hammers home and exceptionally analyses all these ideas. It's a powerful film. A powerful fim that wraps up it's story with an outstandingly tragic ending that has stuck with me so long and I think will stick with me forever.

Al inicio de la película me confundí un poco con la cronología de la historia, pero no tardas en captarla. Muy buen papel de Edward Norton. Durante toda la película estuve pensando que sería muy decepcionante si era un cliché de toda la vida donde se arregla el pasado oscuro del protagonista y su entorno sana como si nada hubiera pasado. Boy was I wrong. El final es espectacular, uno de los plot twists más crudos e impactantes que he visto en mucho tiempo. Alrededor de la película tuve el pendiente de que el conflicto entre Danny y Little Henry no se había arreglado, pero hacen tan buen trabajo en disuadirte de ello y enfocarse en el problema que trae Derek con la pandilla que cuando Henry mata a Danny quedas en shock. Es crudo, pero es real. Muchas veces los conflictos más tontos con las peores consecuencias no son fruto más que del orgullo y la soberbia. El personaje de Derek es muy trágico, a pesar de haber hecho todo bien cuando cayó en la realización y después de reivindicarse, al final perdió a quien más quería sin poder evitarlo. Casi para terminar es reconfortante cómo la relación de Derek y Lamont se desarrolla, y ver como una persona con los gestos más simples puede sacar del hoyo a otra y cambiarla para bien completamente. Por último, acerca de la trama en general, me gusta mucho que la película muestra cómo muchas personas que son pertenecientes a cultos de odio son influenciadas desde sus raíces y ambiente a pensar así y les es muy difícil evitarlo, como es el caso de Derek y por consiguiente Danny. Sin nada más que agregar… Algunas escenas muy buenas: -La comida de la familia de Derek: Me gusta porque muestra como las ideologías de odio pueden destrozar ambientes con extrema facilidad. -El crimen y arresto de Derek: Enseña la deshumanización que puede pasar una persona a causa del odio. La escena es interesante porque en ningún momento del proceso Derek muestra remordimiento, cuando lo esposan se ve enojado y frustrado, pero nunca arrepentido de lo que hizo. -El final: Simplemente es cine. Calificación final: 9.3/10, en lo personal se me hizo buenísima, pero no es fácil de ver. Toca temas muy sensibles, hay violencia y sobre todo mucho odio. Puedo entender porque puede ser difícil para algunas personas. Canción con la que la asocio: We better Learn To Hotwire An Uterus - The Fall of Troy. Como la película, cruda, frenética y violenta, con un final amargo. Gracias por la recomendación Chila.
Dura como pocas: las raíces del odio y lo que cuesta salir de él. Edward Norton hace un papel que pesa años después. El blanco y negro le queda como advertencia.

« has anything you’ve done made your life better ? » There are films that move us because of what they tell us, and others that move us because of what they force us to confront. American History X undoubtedly belongs to the latter. What fascinates me about this film is that it never tries to make hatred incomprehensible. On the contrary, it shows us how it is built, how it takes root, and how it eventually becomes an identity. Derek wasn’t born hateful. He learned to be. And perhaps that’s the most terrifying part: realizing that the most destructive ideologies aren’t necessarily born out of monsters, but can also emerge from ordinary individuals, shaped by their environment, their frustrations, their grief, and the narratives they choose to believe. I’ve always found the relationship between Derek and Danny particularly heartbreaking. Because beyond the issue of race, this is also a story about inheritance. Hatred passed down almost like a family legacy, an older brother becoming a role model, a teenager desperately trying to become someone he admires. And yet, the very person who helped shape Danny is ultimately the one who realizes he must protect him from the same path. Derek’s journey resonates deeply with me because it isn’t built around some miraculous redemption. Understanding your mistakes doesn’t erase them. Leaving hatred behind doesn’t mean walking away unscathed from everything you’ve inflicted upon others. There’s something profoundly tragic about such a late awakening: realizing that you’ve devoted part of your life to defending an ideology that has done nothing but strip you of your humanity. And then there’s the visual contrast between black and white and colour, which accompanies the narrative so beautifully. The past, with its certainties and almost glorified violence, and then the present, more nuanced, more painful. As though the film were reminding us that reality is always far more complicated than the categories we try to force it into. But what stays with me most is the idea that hatred is a vicious cycle. It claims to protect, to avenge, to restore order; in reality, it only reproduces the very things it claims to fight against. And by the time we finally realize that it leads nowhere, it is sometimes already too late. The ending always leaves me with the same feeling of injustice and helplessness. Because we witness genuine change, an attempt to break a cycle, only to realize that the world doesn’t stop and wait for us to make things right. « Has anything you’ve done made your life better? » Such a simple question, yet probably one of the most devastating lines in the entire film. And perhaps one of the most universal, too. A film that does more than condemn hatred: it tries to understand how it survives, how it is passed down, and why it is so difficult to escape. A film about racism, obviously, but above all, about the human consequences of our convictions when we stop questioning them. I think that’s also why I love it so much. Because it doesn’t give us the comfort of believing that hatred is always something that belongs to other people.
